takeaways: Chip design turns an idea into a complete blueprint, and a chip factory accepts only designs that have passed software from Synopsys, Cadence or Siemens.
Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA took more than 85 percent of the $18 billion market for design software and licensed blocks in 2025.
Tools from the three design flows cannot be combined, and each foundry certifies exact tool versions, so a newcomer would have to write a fourth flow from nothing.
In 2025 Washington cut off design-software sales to China for five weeks, and China still cannot finish a leading-edge design without foreign tools.

cards.q: What does the chip design stage produce?
cards.a: A complete blueprint of where each transistor sits and how it is wired.
cards.why: The whole stage runs in software. A chip factory accepts only designs that have passed tools from Synopsys, Cadence or Siemens.

cards.q: What share of the market for design software and licensed blocks did the three leading vendors hold in 2025?
cards.a: More than 85 percent, split among Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA.
cards.why: The market was worth $18 billion in 2025. No other vendor held more than 5 percent in any core category.

cards.q: Why does a chip team use one vendor's design flow from start to finish?
cards.a: The foundry accepts timing signed off only in the tool it has approved.
cards.why: Each foundry certifies its reference recipes against specific tool versions. A newcomer would have to write a fourth complete flow from nothing.

cards.q: How long did the United States stop design-software sales to China in 2025?
cards.a: Five weeks, from late May to 2 July.
cards.why: Cadence got its letter on 23 May, and the ban ended after trade talks. CSET finds that Chinese vendors still cannot support designs at the leading edge.

takeaways: Every leading-edge chip starts on a 300 mm wafer, a slice of one silicon crystal polished flat enough for extreme-ultraviolet printing to stay in focus across the disc.
Five firms in Japan, Taiwan, Germany and South Korea make these wafers, and none of them is American or Chinese.
Switching wafer suppliers takes two to five years, because a fab must approve each new source separately for every chip it makes.
China made about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2023, but 98 percent of it was solar grade and too impure for chips.

cards.q: Why must a wafer for leading-edge chips be so flat?
cards.a: Extreme-ultraviolet printing stays in focus over only a very small range of heights.
cards.why: The flatness has to hold at every point across a 300 mm disc.

cards.q: Which five firms make the 300 mm wafers for leading-edge chips?
cards.a: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic and SK Siltron.
cards.why: They are headquartered in Japan, Taiwan, Germany and South Korea. None of them is American or Chinese.

cards.q: How long does a fab take to switch to a new wafer supplier?
cards.a: Two to five years.
cards.why: The fab tests each new source separately for every chip it makes.

cards.q: China made about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2023. Why does that give it little hold over chip wafers?
cards.a: About 98 percent of that output was solar grade, too impure for chips.
cards.why: Electronic grade was 2 percent of China's 2023 output. As of 2021 Chinese firms held under 1 percent of the 300 mm wafer market.

takeaways: Photoresist is the light-sensitive coating that holds the printed pattern on the wafer, and a few hundred other gases and liquids deposit, strip and clean layers between steps.
Japan made about 90 percent of the world's photoresist in 2021 and 78 percent in 2023.
Each resist formula is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, so Korea needed five years to build substitutes after Japan's 2019 export licenses.
China's export controls cover gallium, germanium and antimony, which go into optics and non-silicon chips and stay out of a silicon GPU.

cards.q: What does photoresist do in chipmaking?
cards.a: It holds the printed pattern so the next machine can etch it into the wafer.
cards.why: Light changes the resist where it lands, and a wash removes the exposed parts. The pattern left behind guides the etch.

cards.q: Which country makes most of the world's semiconductor photoresist?
cards.a: Japan.
cards.why: Japan made about 90 percent in 2021 and 78 percent in 2023. The United States held 13 percent in 2023.

cards.q: How long did Korea need to replace Japanese photoresist after Japan's 2019 export licenses?
cards.a: Five years.
cards.why: Each resist formula is approved for one layer of one product at one fab. A new supplier works through each fab one layer at a time.

cards.q: Why do China's controls on gallium and germanium do little to stop silicon GPU production?
cards.a: Neither metal goes into a silicon logic chip.
cards.why: Germanium goes into fiber optics and infrared optics, and gallium into the non-silicon wafers behind radio front ends, LEDs and lasers. The controls move prices.

takeaways: Lithography prints each layer of a circuit onto the wafer, and finer lines need shorter light, so the finest layers need extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scanners working in a vacuum.
ASML of the Netherlands builds every EUV scanner in the world and sold 48 of them in 2025.
Zeiss polishes the scanner's mirrors to within tens of picometers, and its optics cap how many EUV scanners ASML can build.
No EUV scanner has ever been sold to a customer in China, and China's answer so far is domestic immersion DUV and an EUV prototype that has printed no chip.

cards.q: Why do the finest layers of a leading-edge chip need an extreme-ultraviolet scanner?
cards.a: Finer lines need light of a shorter wavelength, and EUV light has the shortest.
cards.why: EUV light has a wavelength of 13.5 nm. Glass and air stop it, so the scanner works in a vacuum and focuses with mirrors.

cards.q: How many companies build extreme-ultraviolet scanners?
cards.a: Only one, ASML of the Netherlands.
cards.why: ASML sold 48 EUV systems in 2025. Nikon and Canon make deep ultraviolet scanners and steppers for coarser layers.

cards.q: Which supplier caps how many EUV scanners ASML can build?
cards.a: Zeiss, which polishes and coats the mirrors.
cards.why: Zeiss makes the illumination system and the six-mirror projection optics, with mirrors up to a meter across. Final assembly in Veldhoven waits on those optics.

cards.q: Has China printed a chip with EUV light?
cards.a: No. A prototype in Shenzhen makes EUV light but has printed no chip.
cards.why: Reuters reported the prototype in December 2025. No EUV scanner has ever been sold to a customer in China.

takeaways: A photomask is the stencil for one layer of a chip, and the same plate prints that layer on wafer after wafer, so any flaw repeats on every wafer.
Three firms supply EUV mask blanks worldwide, led by AGC and Hoya of Japan, and only Lasertec of Japan sells a tool that inspects masks in EUV light.
The business is too small to fund a new entrant, which would face twenty years of defect learning to serve a handful of customers.
China has no EUV mask blank, no EUV inspection tool and no multi-beam writer, and SMIC's mask shops serve only older scanners.

cards.q: Why must a photomask be free of defects?
cards.a: One plate prints its layer on wafer after wafer, so any flaw repeats.
cards.why: One plate shapes millions of chips. A speck of dust or a buried particle prints on every wafer until someone finds it.

cards.q: Which firm sells the only tool that inspects an EUV mask in the same light the scanner uses?
cards.a: Lasertec, of Japan.
cards.why: Actinic inspection looks at 13.5 nm, the wavelength the mask itself sees. KLA sells optical reticle inspection, and Zeiss sells e-beam repair.

cards.q: Why has no new firm entered the market for EUV mask blanks?
cards.a: The market is too small to repay twenty years of defect learning.
cards.why: Three firms supply the blanks to a handful of customers. AGC aimed for more than ¥40 billion of annual sales from the business.

cards.q: What kinds of photomask can China make today?
cards.a: Masks for older scanners only.
cards.why: SMIC runs two mask shops in Shanghai for g-line, i-line, KrF and ArF tools. No Chinese firm makes an EUV blank, an actinic inspection tool or a multi-beam writer.

takeaways: Deposition lays down films a few atoms thick, and etch cuts away whatever the printed pattern leaves exposed, in more than a thousand rounds per chip.
Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and ASM International sell most deposition and etch tools, and none of them dominates as ASML does in lithography.
Three or four makers can supply most deposition and etch steps, but switching makers for the newest chips takes two to five years of testing.
Chinese makers reached about 11 percent of dry etch by 2024 and stayed under 1 percent of atomic layer deposition, which gate-all-around logic depends on.

cards.q: How do deposition and etch work together to build a chip?
cards.a: Deposition lays down a thin film, and etch removes what the pattern leaves exposed.
cards.why: Lithography prints the pattern between the two steps. A chip takes more than a thousand of these rounds.

cards.q: Which four firms sell most deposition and etch tools?
cards.a: Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and ASM International.
cards.why: Each leads different tool families, such as Lam in conductor etch and ASM International in atomic layer deposition. None dominates as ASML does in lithography.

cards.q: How long does a fab take to switch deposition or etch tool makers for its newest chips?
cards.a: Two to five years of testing the new tool on the fab's own line.
cards.why: Three or four makers can supply most deposition and etch steps. The new tool has to match the old one before the fab uses it for production.

cards.q: In which kind of deposition and etch tool have Chinese makers gained least?
cards.a: Atomic layer deposition, where they stayed under 1 percent.
cards.why: Between 2019 and 2024 China-based suppliers rose to about 11 percent of dry etch and 7 percent of deposition. Gate-all-around logic depends on atomic layer deposition.

takeaways: Metrology and inspection tools check each wafer between steps for line width, layer alignment and defects, which is how a fab learns why its chips fail.
KLA of the United States holds about 57 percent of the process control tool market, six to seven times its nearest rival, and its share is still growing.
A bigger chip is a bigger target for a stray speck, so AI accelerators, among the largest chips cut from a wafer, depend most on finding defects.
Chinese firms held 0.7 percent of the process control tool market in 2025, their weakest position in any major kind of chipmaking tool.

cards.q: What do metrology and inspection tools do in a fab?
cards.a: They check each wafer between steps for line width, alignment and defects.
cards.why: Their measurements show the fab why its chips fail.

cards.q: What share of the process control tool market does KLA hold?
cards.a: About 57 percent, six to seven times its nearest rival.
cards.why: CSET puts KLA at 56.8 percent of a $15.7 billion market in 2025. KLA says its share is still rising, and nobody else reaches 11 percent.

cards.q: Why does finding defects matter most for AI accelerators?
cards.a: They are among the largest chips, and a bigger chip is a bigger target.
cards.why: For an 8 square centimeter die, halving the defect density lifts yield from about 49 percent to about 69 percent.

cards.q: What share of the process control tool market did Chinese firms hold in 2025?
cards.a: 0.7 percent.
cards.why: That is their weakest position in any major kind of chipmaking tool. Without sensitive inspection, a fab cannot find out why its yield is low.

takeaways: The front end builds the transistors, and wrapping the gate around all four sides of each channel stops current leaking when the switch is off.
Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung can build 2 nm-class gate-all-around transistors, and only TSMC runs such a process at volume for outside customers.
The scarce asset is the process recipe, meaning which steps run in which order on which tools, and no firm sells its recipe.
SMIC reaches 5 nm-class features without EUV by printing each layer in several passes, which still leaves China behind the newest chips.

cards.q: Why do the newest transistors wrap the gate around all four sides of the channel?
cards.a: To stop a short channel leaking current when the switch is off.
cards.why: A shorter channel switches faster and packs tighter. A gate on every side can shut the flow off completely.

cards.q: Which companies can build a 2 nm-class gate-all-around transistor?
cards.a: TSMC, Intel and Samsung.
cards.why: Only TSMC runs such a process at volume for outside customers. Rapidus targets 2 nm mass production in 2027.

cards.q: What makes the front end a chokepoint?
cards.a: The process recipe, meaning which steps run in which order on which tools.
cards.why: Three firms have written a recipe for the newest transistors, and none sells it. A newcomer has to work out its own.

cards.q: How does SMIC reach 5 nm-class features without an extreme-ultraviolet scanner?
cards.a: It prints each layer in several passes on deep-ultraviolet tools.
cards.why: SMIC builds 7 and 5 nm-class nodes this way. CSIS judges that China still cannot build a working EUV system.

takeaways: A foundry makes chips for other companies on shared tools, because no chip company sells enough of one product to fill a fab costing tens of billions of dollars.
TSMC leads the foundries, and all six of its largest plants, which hold 13 of its 17 million wafers a year, are in Taiwan.
Money can buy a fab building, and the slow part is a workforce that has run one process for years, so a working line takes five to ten years.
China has more fab capacity than any other region, and almost none of it can make the newest chips.

cards.q: Why do chip companies share foundries?
cards.a: No single chip company sells enough of one product to fill a fab.
cards.why: A fab costs tens of billions of dollars. BCG puts the ten-year cost of one finished in 2026 at $35 to $43 billion.

cards.q: Where are TSMC's six largest plants, the gigafabs?
cards.a: All six are in Taiwan.
cards.why: Each runs more than 100,000 wafers a month. Together they hold 13 of TSMC's 17 million wafers a year.

cards.q: What is the slow part of moving leading-edge chipmaking out of Taiwan?
cards.a: Training a workforce that has run one process for years.
cards.why: Money can buy the building. TSMC has committed $165 billion to the United States and has yet to build a gigafab outside Taiwan.

cards.q: How does China's fab capacity compare with other regions?
cards.a: China has the most of any region, and almost none of it is advanced.
cards.why: SEMI forecast China at 10.1 million wafers a month in 2025, against Taiwan's 5.8 million. SMIC cannot buy an EUV scanner, so it cannot make the newest chips.

takeaways: HBM stacks memory chips into a cube wired through copper-filled holes, and its speed and size usually set how many users one AI chip can serve.
SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make every HBM stack in the world, and the two Korean firms sold 82.5 percent of it in 2025.
A new HBM maker would need the newest DRAM, a line that thins and stacks chips without warping, and a pass on Nvidia's test, which takes five to ten years.
A US export control catches every HBM stack now in production, and no Chinese firm ships HBM3E or HBM4 in volume.

cards.q: Why does memory speed matter so much when an AI chip answers a prompt?
cards.a: For each word, the chip reads the whole model from memory and does little arithmetic.
cards.why: The chip then waits for the next read. Memory size and speed usually set how many users one chip can serve.

cards.q: Which firms make every HBM stack in the world?
cards.a: SK hynix, Samsung and Micron.
cards.why: SK hynix took 63.2 percent of 2025 HBM revenue, Samsung 19.3 and Micron 17.4. TSMC builds the logic base die for SK hynix's HBM4 and makes no stacks.

cards.q: What two capabilities would a fourth HBM maker need inside one company?
cards.a: Leading-edge DRAM and a line that thins and stacks chips.
cards.why: Nobody outside the three has both. The finished stack would then have to pass Nvidia's qualification test, and the whole effort takes five to ten years.

cards.q: Which HBM stacks now in production fall under the US export control?
cards.a: Every one of them.
cards.why: ECCN 3A090.c covers HBM above 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter, and every stack in production exceeds it. The rule also reaches stacks made abroad with American technology.

takeaways: An AI accelerator needs more circuit than a scanner prints in one shot, so packaging joins several chips and their memory on a shared silicon interposer.
TSMC packages nearly every AI accelerator with its CoWoS process in Taiwan, and Nvidia alone took an estimated 60.3 percent of CoWoS in 2025.
Each packaging step is ordinary on its own, and the hard part is making enough working packages at volume, which capped AI chip output in 2024 and 2025.
China packages chips at scale but has no silicon-interposer packaging at volume, and American CoWoS-class capacity starts only in 2028.

cards.q: Why is an AI accelerator built from several chips in one package?
cards.a: It needs more circuit than a scanner can print in one exposure.
cards.why: A scanner prints at most 858 mm2 in one shot. Packaging sets the pieces and their memory side by side on a silicon interposer and wires them together.

cards.q: Which firm packages nearly every leading AI accelerator?
cards.a: TSMC, with its CoWoS process in Taiwan.
cards.why: Nvidia alone took an estimated 60.3 percent of CoWoS in 2025. Outsourced firms such as ASE, Amkor and JCET handle the rest of the packaging market.

cards.q: Why did packaging cap AI chip output through 2024 and 2025?
cards.a: Too few packaging lines had been built.
cards.why: Each step is ordinary on its own, but one cracked joint scraps a whole package. By March 2026 the constraint had moved back to front-end wafers.

cards.q: When does CoWoS-class packaging start in the United States?
cards.a: In early 2028, at Amkor's plant in Peoria, Arizona.
cards.why: Amkor is building a $7B plant there with up to $407M of CHIPS Act money. No firm yet does CoWoS-class packaging in volume in the United States.

takeaways: A package substrate is the layered adapter that carries signals from a chip's hair-fine connections down to a circuit board wired in millimeters.
Ajinomoto of Japan puts its share of the insulating film inside high-end packages at about 95 percent, and Nitto Boseki of Japan leads in the glass cloth beneath it.
Money can expand substrate plants, and a replacement film would need approval in each layer of each product at every substrate maker, which takes five to ten years.
No American firm makes these substrates in volume, and Chinese firms make almost none of the high-end film, though they are pushing into glass cloth.

cards.q: What job does a package substrate do?
cards.a: It links the chip's hair-fine connections to a circuit board wired in millimeters.
cards.why: It is built in layers of epoxy film and copper around a stiff glass-cloth core. Copper in laser-drilled holes carries signals from layer to layer.

cards.q: Which company makes most of the insulating film inside high-end chip packages?
cards.a: Ajinomoto, a Japanese food company.
cards.why: Ajinomoto puts its share of the film at about 95 percent, and its film has been the standard since 1999.

cards.q: How long would replacing Ajinomoto's film take?
cards.a: Five to ten years.
cards.why: Every substrate maker and packaging house has to approve a new film in each layer of each product. That takes years at each of them.

cards.q: How many American firms make package substrates in volume?
cards.a: None.
cards.why: The White House named eight substrate makers in its 2021 supply chain review, and none is American. Chinese firms make almost none of the high-end film.

takeaways: Test puts electricity through each chip at several stages, so a bad die is caught before it can ruin a package holding a dozen expensive pieces.
Advantest of Japan sold about 65 percent of chip testers in 2025, and together with Teradyne of the United States it holds about 80 percent.
Every test and assembly tool has more than one maker, and switching testers is slow because it means rebuilding every test program.
Assembly and test is China's strongest stage, with four of the top ten firms, and its tools are far less tightly controlled than lithography tools.

cards.q: Why does the industry now test chips sooner, hotter and longer than it used to?
cards.a: One bad die can ruin a package holding a dozen expensive pieces.
cards.why: Wafer sort, burn-in, final test and system-level test each catch failures the round before cannot see.

cards.q: Which firm sells most of the world's chip testers?
cards.a: Advantest, of Japan.
cards.why: Advantest puts its share at about 65 percent of a $9.0 billion tester market in 2025. With Teradyne, the second maker, it holds about 80 percent.

cards.q: Why do chip customers rarely switch tester makers?
cards.a: A new tester means rebuilding every test program.
cards.why: Each program is built from the first prototype through to the production line, and a switch repeats all of that work.

cards.q: At which stage of the chain is China most competitive?
cards.a: Assembly and test.
cards.why: CSET counts four of the top ten assembly and test firms by 2024 revenue as Chinese. Their tools are far less tightly controlled than lithography or deposition tools.

takeaways: AI chips are wired into racks of 72 that run as one computer, with copper links inside each rack and lasers sending light down glass fiber beyond it.
Rack assembly is competitive, and if Foxconn stopped, Quanta and Wistron could take over its volume within a few quarters.
The hardest parts to replace are NVLink-class switching, which only Nvidia sells at that bandwidth, and the indium phosphide lasers for the optical links.
American firms make the switch chips and lasers, while Chinese firms assemble high-speed optical modules in volume and China produces about 70 percent of the world's indium.

cards.q: Why do the longer links in an AI cluster carry signals as light down glass fiber?
cards.a: Copper carries these signals only a few meters before they fade.
cards.why: Inside a rack the trays reach each other over copper. A laser at one end of each longer link turns the electrical signal into pulses of light.

cards.q: Which firms could take over if Foxconn stopped assembling AI racks?
cards.a: Quanta and Wistron, within a few quarters.
cards.why: Contract manufacturers on three continents build racks, and the power shelves, busbars, cables and connectors have many suppliers.

cards.q: Which two parts of an AI rack are hardest to replace?
cards.a: NVLink-class switching and indium phosphide lasers.
cards.why: Only Nvidia sells a scale-up switch with NVLink's bandwidth to all comers. Nvidia put $2 billion each into Coherent and Lumentum to secure laser capacity.

cards.q: What share of the world's indium does China produce?
cards.a: About 70 percent.
cards.why: Indium is the raw material for the lasers in optical links. Chinese firms such as InnoLight and Eoptolink also assemble high-speed optical modules in volume.

takeaways: A data center feeds power to its racks and carries their heat away, and one AI rack draws up to 142 kilowatts, more heat than air can remove.
Power equipment now sets the pace of a buildout, and a large power transformer takes about 36 months to arrive, against under a year before 2020.
Several vendors sell every piece of power and cooling equipment, and money still cannot shorten the queues for transformers and turbines.
China has spare generating capacity and is limited by accelerators, while the United States imports most large power transformers and waits years for them.

cards.q: Why are new AI racks cooled with water?
cards.a: A 142 kW rack gives off more heat than air can carry away.
cards.why: Every watt a rack draws comes back out as heat. Cold plates on the GPU packages pass it to a building water loop that releases it outdoors.

cards.q: How long does a large power transformer now take to arrive?
cards.a: About 36 months.
cards.why: The worst lead times reach 60 months. Before 2020 the wait was under a year.

cards.q: What part of a data center buildout can money not speed up?
cards.a: The wait for transformers and gas turbines.
cards.why: Several vendors sell every piece of power and cooling equipment. GE Vernova has close to six years of gas turbine orders booked.

cards.q: What limits China's AI data center buildout?
cards.a: The supply of accelerators.
cards.why: China has spare generating capacity and its own transformer and switchgear industry.

takeaways: Building a Blackwell B200 costs about $6,400, and Nvidia sells it for $30,000 to $40,000.
High-bandwidth memory is the largest line in the build, about 45 percent, while the logic dies are about 14 percent.
Packaging and its scrap cost more than twice the logic dies, because a package that fails after the memory goes on throws away the dies and the memory.
Three firms make the memory and one Taiwanese firm does the packaging, and in 2026 the memory maker Micron reported a higher gross margin than Nvidia.

cards.q: What does a Blackwell B200 cost to build?
cards.a: About $6,400.
cards.why: Epoch AI's estimate ranges from $5,700 to $7,300. Nvidia sells the chip for $30,000 to $40,000.

cards.q: Which part is the largest line in the cost of building a B200?
cards.a: The high-bandwidth memory, about 45 percent of the build.
cards.why: The 192 GB of HBM3E costs about $2,900. The two logic dies cost about $900.

cards.q: Why does packaging yield add so much to the cost of a B200?
cards.a: A package that fails after the memory goes on scraps the dies and the memory.
cards.why: Packaging yield runs 65 to 95 percent. Scrap adds roughly $1,000 to every B200 that ships, on top of about $1,100 for CoWoS-L packaging.

cards.q: Which firm reported a higher gross margin than Nvidia in 2026?
cards.a: Micron, the memory maker.
cards.why: Micron reported 84.6 percent in the quarter to May 2026, against 75.0 percent at Nvidia. Assembly and test firms earned 17 to 21 percent.

takeaways: An export control works only when a country's own firms sell something the buyer cannot get elsewhere, so only a few countries can use one on chips.
Since 2020 Washington has built its controls one rule at a time, reaching foreign goods made with US technology and, from 2022, whole countries.
The controls have kept China below the leading edge, and Chinese tool vendors still took 35 percent of their home market in 2025.
Taiwan holds 78 percent of the world's contract chipmaking, and no policy so far has moved leading-edge logic or packaging off the island.

cards.q: When does an export control have real effect?
cards.a: When a country's own firms sell something the buyer cannot get elsewhere.
cards.why: The machines, software and chemicals for an advanced chip come from a short list of firms in the United States, the Netherlands, Japan and South Korea.

cards.q: What did the Foreign Direct Product Rule of August 2020 change?
cards.a: It reached foreign items made with US technology and bound for Huawei.
cards.why: Huawei had turned to foreign chips after its 2019 Entity List listing. The rule let American controls reach chips made abroad.
cards.section: The US export-control campaign, 2018 to today

cards.q: What share of their home market did Chinese chipmaking-tool vendors take in 2025?
cards.a: 35 percent.
cards.why: China still sits below the leading edge. SMIC prints 7 nm-class logic without an EUV scanner, and a shortage of memory stacks caps Ascend output.

cards.q: Where does 2 nm chipmaking run today?
cards.a: Only in Taiwan.
cards.why: Taiwan bars overseas production of its most advanced chips, so TSMC's American fabs run a generation behind. Taiwan's foundries hold 78 percent of contract chipmaking.
